passage: After Thursday's talk, with the release deadline pressing, Pooja wrote the plan that evening. Three goals: finish tickets by their dates, add tests to every change, and ask for help within an hour of getting stuck. Under them, the support: a fifteen-minute check-in each morning, Nitin as pairing partner, and a review on the fourteenth of next month, six weeks away. She also wrote plainly what would happen if the goals weren't met: a conversation with the manager about whether the role fits. Next morning she gave it to Yogesh, who read it twice and asked two questions. Both signed at the bottom. "It's clear," Yogesh said. "At least I know where I stand."

subtype: Approach: written improvement plan with a review date [Action]
passage:
The morning after their difficult talk, Shankar sat in the corner cabin of the Mumbai ad agency and typed up what they'd agreed.
He kept it to one page. Three goals for Urmila: first drafts of client copy by Wednesday each week; no more than one round of spelling corrections per draft; present her own idea in at least two client meetings. Then the support: a thirty-minute review with him every Friday, and a copywriting course the agency would pay for. At the bottom: "Review date: 15 August, six weeks from today. If the goals are met, the plan closes. If not, we'll discuss next steps, which may include a formal performance process."
He printed two copies and handed one to Urmila.
She read it slowly. "Can I change 'two meetings' to 'two presentations'? Meetings sometimes get cancelled."
"Fair." He changed it.
They both signed. Urmila folded her copy carefully into her notebook.

qa.q: What might Urmila have been feeling as she folded her copy into her notebook?
qa.a: She may have felt nervous about the goals but also reassured, because the expectations and support were clear and she had been able to change one word.

qa.q: What else could Shankar do between now and the review date?
qa.a: He could use the Friday reviews to note progress on each goal in writing, so the August review has no surprises.

qa.q: How does the written plan look from Urmila's side?
qa.a: It feels firm but fair: she knows exactly what is expected, what help she gets and what happens if goals aren't met, and her suggestion was accepted.

grounding: It shows a lead writing three goals, the support offered and a six-week review date, with both signing so expectations and consequences are clear.

subtype: Approach: written improvement plan with a review date [Action]
passage:
"Rehana, I've written up what we discussed yesterday. Can you read it with me?"
Shalini slid a single sheet across the table in the quiet meeting room.
"Three goals," Rehana read aloud. "Close tickets within two days. Update the customer notes every time. Handle refunds without escalating unless it's above the limit."
"And below that?"
"Support. A weekly half hour with you. Shadowing Bhanu on refunds for two weeks." Rehana looked up. "And we meet again after six weeks."
"Yes. On the 3rd of May. If you've met the goals, we close this. If not, we talk about next steps honestly. I don't want any surprises for either of us."
Rehana was quiet for a moment. "It's strange seeing it on paper. But it's clearer than just feeling I'm doing badly."
"Anything you'd change?"
"Can refunds be the last goal? It's the hardest."
"Yes." Shalini changed the order. They both signed.

qa.q: Who will Rehana shadow on refunds?
How did Rehana feel seeing the goals on paper?
qa.a: Rehana found it strange and a bit uncomfortable at first but also relieved, since the page was clearer than a vague sense of doing badly.

qa.q: What else could Shalini add to make the plan fairer?
qa.a: Shalini could agree a short midway check at three weeks, so Rehana knows early whether things are on track.

qa.q: How might the plan look from Shalini's side?
qa.a: Shalini has clear, agreed goals to judge in May, so Shalini can be honest with Rehana without the review feeling like a surprise.

grounding: It shows a lead writing three goals, the support offered and a six-week review, with both signing so expectations and consequences are clear and fair.
